blocks.text: You know that there are two basic types of cell, prokaryotic and eukaryotic. All bacteria are prokaryotes. Yeast and Euglena are examples of unicellular eukaryotes; plants and animals are multicellular eukaryotes. Eukaryotic cells are more complex than prokaryotic cells. This topic studies the structures present in cells and their functions.
Cell wall

The cell wall is a more or less solid layer surrounding a cell. It is found in bacteria, fungi, plants and algae. When a cell wall is removed using cell-wall-degrading enzymes, the remaining components of the cell are called a protoplast.

The primary wall is the actual cell wall of the cell. It is composed of polysaccharides: cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin. The cellulose microfibrils are aligned at all angles and are held together by hydrogen bonds. Many proteins are also present in primary walls. The middle lamella is a gelatinous layer that separates and holds the primary walls of neighbouring cells. It is laid first, formed from the cell plate during cytokinesis, and the primary cell wall is then expanded inside the middle lamella. It contains magnesium and calcium pectates (salts of pectic acid). In some plant cells, after maturation, a secondary wall is made between the protoplast and the primary wall. Secondary cell walls contain lignin, cellulose and hemicellulose; because of the lignin, the secondary wall is more rigid than the primary wall.

blocks.title: Plasmodesmata (singular plasmodesma)
blocks.text: Small channels that directly connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring plant cells. They penetrate both the primary and secondary cell walls and allow certain molecules to pass directly from one cell to another, so they are important in cellular communication. They form during cell division when parts of the endoplasmic reticulum of the parent cell get trapped in the new cell wall.

blocks.alt: Two plant cells side by side with their shared wall drawn in cross-section: from the outside in, the middle lamella in the centre, a primary wall on each side with cellulose microfibrils at various angles, a dark secondary wall, then each cell's plasma membrane. A channel (plasmodesma) crosses all the layers and joins the two cytoplasms, with a strand of ER inside it.
blocks.caption: The walls of two neighbouring plant cells and a plasmodesma (original diagram after Figures 3.5 and 3.6).
blocks.long_description: The middle lamella of magnesium and calcium pectates is laid first and is shared by both cells. Each cell then builds its primary wall of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin inside the middle lamella, and after maturation a lignified secondary wall inside that. The plasma membrane lines the inside of the wall. The plasmodesma is a membrane-lined channel through all the wall layers that connects the cytoplasm of one cell to the other.

blocks.title: A debate about cell theory
blocks.text: Plasmodesmata have caused debate among scientists: some suggest that the cells of higher plants are not really separate cells, since they are not physically separated or independent from one another.

Cell walls have a number of functions. They provide rigidity to the cell for structural and mechanical support; they maintain cell shape and the direction of cell growth, and ultimately the architecture of the plant; the cell wall prevents expansion when water enters the cell; it protects against pathogens and the environment; and it is a store of carbohydrates for the plant.

blocks.caption: Cell walls in different groups
rows: Cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin (primary); lignin added in secondary walls
Cellulose and a variety of glycoproteins
Silica, made from silicic acid polymerised inside the cell and then extruded; cheaper in energy, which is why diatoms grow fast
Chitin, the same carbohydrate that strengthens insect exoskeletons
Peptidoglycan, a single large polymer of amino acids and sugar
Different polysaccharides and proteins; no peptidoglycan

blocks.text: Plasma membrane
All prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have a plasma membrane that encloses their contents and serves as a semi-porous barrier to the outside environment.
Structure of the plasma membrane

The fluid mosaic model is the widely accepted concept that describes the dynamic nature of the plasma membrane. It was proposed by two American biologists, S. J. Singer and Garth Nicolson, in 1972. According to the fluid mosaic model, the basic foundation of the plasma membrane is a lipid bilayer made of phospholipids, and a collection of proteins floats within this bilayer.

Each phospholipid has a phosphate group at one end of the molecule. Phospholipids are hydrophilic ("water-loving") at their phosphate ends and hydrophobic ("water-fearing") along their tail regions, which contain C-H chains. In the lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane the hydrophobic tails are oriented inwards and the hydrophilic phosphate groups are aligned outwards, towards either the cytoplasm or the extracellular environment.

In eukaryotes, plasma membranes have cholesterol molecules wedged into the phospholipid bilayer; they keep the membrane fluid at low temperatures. Many proteins float within the bilayer, while some other proteins simply adhere to its surfaces. The positioning of proteins is related to the organisation of the cytoskeleton.

blocks.alt: A cross-section of the plasma membrane: two rows of phospholipids with blue heads facing out and yellow tails facing in. Embedded in it from left to right are a channel protein with a pore, a carrier protein, a receptor protein with a messenger molecule bound on the outside, a peripheral protein on the inner surface, a cholesterol molecule wedged between tails, and a glycoprotein with a sugar chain outside. A glycolipid with a short sugar chain sits at the left.
blocks.caption: The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane (original diagram after Figures 3.7 and 3.8).
blocks.long_description: The phospholipid bilayer has hydrophilic heads facing the water on both sides and hydrophobic tails inside. Proteins float in the bilayer: channel proteins and carrier proteins transport substances; receptor proteins bind messengers such as hormones; peripheral proteins attach the membrane to the cytoskeleton; glycoproteins and glycolipids carry sugar chains on the outside that serve as identification marks. Cholesterol wedged between the tails keeps the membrane fluid when it is cold.

blocks.text: Plasma membrane proteins function in several different ways.

items: Many proteins play a role in the selective transport of certain substances across the phospholipid bilayer, acting either as channels or as active transport molecules.
Some proteins help in the attachment of the plasma membrane to the cytoskeleton and to external fibres.
Some proteins on the exterior surface attach to sugars and make identification marks.
Other proteins function as receptors, which bind messenger molecules (for example hormones) and transmit signals to the interior of the cell.
Some proteins also exhibit enzymatic activity, catalysing various reactions related to the plasma membrane.

blocks.title: Why a membrane needs proteins
blocks.text: The interior of the lipid bilayer is hydrophobic and repels water-soluble molecules that try to pass through it. If a cell were fully encased in pure lipid bilayer it would be completely impermeable to water-soluble molecules such as sugars and polar amino acids. That is why, in addition to phospholipids, membranes contain proteins that provide passageways across the membrane.

The outside surface of the plasma membrane has chains of sugars bonded to proteins and lipids. A protein with an attached sugar is a glycoprotein; a lipid with an attached sugar is a glycolipid. The glycoproteins and glycolipids vary from species to species, from individual to individual in the same species, and even from one cell type to another in the same individual. Collectively called the glycocalyx, they function as cell identification marks that are recognised by other cells.

blocks.title: Why identification marks matter
blocks.text: The ability to distinguish among different cells is crucial to life. It allows the cells of an embryo to sort themselves into tissues and organs, and it helps the cells of the immune system to recognise and reject foreign cells, such as infectious bacteria.
Functions of the plasma membrane

Plasma membranes serve as semi-porous barriers to the outside environment. The membrane acts as a boundary, holding the cell constituents together. It is permeable to specific molecules: it allows nutrients and other essential elements to enter the cell and waste materials to leave. Small molecules such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and water pass freely across the membrane, but the passage of larger molecules such as amino acids and sugars is carefully regulated. Eukaryotic cells also have membranes around some of their interior organelles; like the plasma membrane, these regulate the flow of materials into and out of the organelles.
Techniques to study the structure of the plasma membrane

items: Transmission electron microscopy reveals detailed structures of the lipid bilayer and its associated proteins.
Scanning electron microscopy examines the surface topology of cells and membranes.
Confocal microscopy uses laser scanning and fluorescence to create sharp, detailed images of the cell membrane.
Total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy gives high-resolution images of the membrane and its interactions with the cytoskeleton and other cellular components.
Atomic force microscopy provides topographical images of the cell membrane at high resolution.
X-ray crystallography determines the atomic structure of membrane proteins.
Lipidomics is the comprehensive analysis of the lipids in the membrane, using techniques like mass spectrometry.

Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching studies the mobility and dynamics of membrane proteins and lipids: a fluorescently labelled region of the membrane is bleached with a laser and the recovery of fluorescence is observed as unbleached molecules move into the area.

blocks.text: Cytoplasm and organelles

A cell consists of three major components: the plasma membrane, the cytoplasm and the nucleus. The cytoplasm is a semi-viscous, semi-transparent substance. In eukaryotic cells it lies between the plasma membrane and the nuclear envelope; in prokaryotic cells it fills all the space beneath the plasma membrane. It consists of an aqueous ground substance, the cytosol, which contains a variety of organelles and other inclusions. The cytosol is water in which many organic substances (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids) and inorganic salts are completely or partially dissolved. The cytoplasm provides space for the proper functioning of the organelles and is the site of various biochemical (metabolic) reactions, for example glycolysis, the breakdown of glucose during aerobic respiration.
The cytoplasm contains discrete structures specific for various cellular functions, the cell organelles. Organelles are generally enclosed by a membrane, except a few such as the ribosome.

blocks.alt: A rectangular plant cell with a thick outer cell wall and a plasma membrane inside it. A large central vacuole fills the middle. The nucleus with its nucleolus is pushed to one side, with rough ER and smooth ER near it. Three chloroplasts with stacked discs, two mitochondria, a Golgi stack, free ribosomes, a peroxisome and a plasmodesma through the wall are labelled.
blocks.caption: Ultrastructure of a plant cell (original diagram after Figure 3.9).
blocks.long_description: The plant cell is enclosed by a cell wall outside the plasma membrane. Its large central vacuole takes up most of the volume and pushes the nucleus to the side. The nucleus is surrounded by a double envelope and contains a nucleolus. Rough ER with ribosomes and smooth ER lie near the nucleus; the Golgi apparatus is a stack of curved sacs; mitochondria have folded inner membranes; chloroplasts contain stacks of thylakoids. Ribosomes are scattered in the cytoplasm, a peroxisome is a small single-membraned body, and a plasmodesma crosses the wall to the neighbouring cell. There are no centrioles.

blocks.alt: A rounded animal cell bounded by a plasma membrane only. The nucleus with its nucleolus sits at the centre. Rough ER hugs the nucleus on one side and smooth ER lies on the other. Two mitochondria, a Golgi stack, two lysosomes, a peroxisome, a small vacuole, free ribosomes, dotted cytoskeleton lines and a pair of centrioles at right angles are labelled.
blocks.caption: Ultrastructure of an animal cell (original diagram after Figure 3.10).
blocks.long_description: The animal cell has no wall and no chloroplasts. The nucleus is central. Rough ER studded with ribosomes and smooth ER without them connect to the nuclear envelope. The Golgi apparatus packages products; lysosomes hold digestive enzymes; peroxisomes hold oxidative enzymes; vacuoles are small; mitochondria make ATP. A pair of centrioles lies at right angles near the nucleus, and protein fibres of the cytoskeleton run through the cytoplasm.

blocks.text: 1. Nucleus

A prominent nucleus is present in all eukaryotic cells: at the centre in animal cells, pushed to the side in plant cells. The spherical nucleus typically occupies about 10 percent of a eukaryotic cell's volume. It serves as the information-processing and administrative centre of the cell, performing two major functions: it stores the cell's hereditary material (DNA) and it coordinates the cell's activities, such as growth, protein synthesis and cell division. The semifluid matrix inside the nucleus is the nucleoplasm. Within it, most of the nuclear material is chromatin, which organises to form chromosomes during cell division. The nucleus also contains one or more nucleoli, which synthesise ribosomes.
The nuclear envelope and nuclear pores

The nuclear envelope is a double-layered membrane that encloses the contents of the nucleus during most of the cell's life cycle. The space between the two layers, the perinuclear space, is connected with the rough endoplasmic reticulum. During cell division the nuclear envelope disintegrates, but it re-forms in the daughter cells. On the inner side of the envelope there is a protein lining, the nuclear lamina, which binds to chromatin and gives it structural support.

The nuclear envelope has tiny holes, the nuclear pores, which regulate the passage of molecules between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. Nuclear pores are permeable to small molecules, and some larger proteins, such as histones, are also allowed into the nucleus. A nuclear pore is made of an elaborate structure called the nuclear pore complex, composed of several subunits: the annular subunit (surrounding the inside of the pore), the column subunit (making the wall of the complex), the ring subunit (attached to the outer side of the column subunit) and the lumenal subunit (anchoring the pore complex into the nuclear envelope). Tiny fibrils usually extend from the complex and make a basket-like structure on the nuclear side.

blocks.title: What crosses the nuclear envelope
blocks.text: The building blocks of DNA and RNA, and ATP, are allowed to enter the nucleus. Ribosomal subunits, built in the nucleoli, are examples of materials allowed to leave the nucleus and enter the cytoplasm.

blocks.alt: A round nucleus in cross-section: a double envelope with a pale perinuclear space between the two membranes, four nuclear pore complexes drawn as orange gaps in the envelope, a dotted nuclear lamina lining the inside, wavy chromatin fibres in the nucleoplasm, a dark round nucleolus, and rough ER with ribosomes continuing from the outer membrane on the right.
blocks.caption: The nucleus, its envelope, the nuclear pore complexes and the nucleolus (original diagram after Figures 3.11 to 3.13).
blocks.long_description: The nuclear envelope is two membranes with the perinuclear space between them; the outer membrane is continuous with the rough ER. Nuclear pore complexes cross both membranes and control traffic in and out, with a basket of fibrils on the nuclear side. The nuclear lamina, a protein lining inside the envelope, binds the chromatin. The nucleoplasm holds dispersed chromatin (DNA with histone proteins) and the nucleolus, which assembles ribosomal subunits at the nucleolus organiser regions.

blocks.text: Nucleolus

The nucleolus is a prominent, darkly stained structure in the nucleoplasm; there may be one or two nucleoli in a nucleus. Nucleoli manufacture the subunits that combine to form ribosomes. They form at certain sites on chromosomes called nucleolus organiser regions (NORs); the DNA at the NORs encodes ribosomal RNA (rRNA). The nucleolus consists of granular and fibrillar components and DNA. The granules are ribosomal subunits that have already been formed; the fibrils are the raw materials of ribosome subunits, that is rRNA molecules and associated proteins.

blocks.title: Nucleolus size and division
blocks.text: In cells that produce large amounts of protein, and therefore need many ribosomes, the nucleolus is considerably large. At the onset of mitosis the single nucleolus disappears, and after division a new nucleolus forms from the NORs.
Chromatin and chromosomes

The nucleus contains string-like fibres, collectively called chromatin, composed of DNA and proteins. Chromatin is made of a series of bead-like structures called nucleosomes; in a nucleosome the DNA strand wraps around groups of small proteins called histones. During interphase, when the cell is carrying out its normal functions, the chromatin is dispersed throughout the nucleus as a tangle of fibres. When the cell begins to divide, all the chromatin strands are compressed into specialised structures, the chromosomes. A chromosome is made of arms, called chromatids, and a central point, the centromere.

blocks.alt: Four stages from left to right joined by arrows: a DNA double helix; the DNA wound around orange histone beads to make nucleosomes; a coiled chromatin fibre; and an X-shaped chromosome of two chromatids joined at an orange centromere.
blocks.caption: Condensation of chromatin into a chromosome (original diagram after Figure 3.14).
blocks.long_description: DNA, about 2 nm wide, wraps around groups of histone proteins to form bead-like nucleosomes. The beaded string coils into the chromatin fibre that is dispersed through the nucleus during interphase. When the cell divides, the fibre condenses into a chromosome made of two chromatids joined at the centromere. Euchromatin is genetically active and transcribed; heterochromatin is inactive.

blocks.title: Two kinds of chromatin
blocks.text: Euchromatin is the genetically active chromatin involved in transcribing RNA to produce proteins. Heterochromatin is the other kind; its DNA is genetically inactive. Inside the nucleus of every human cell there is about 6 feet of DNA, divided into 46 molecules, each about 1.5 inches long, one for each chromosome.

The number of chromosomes in the nuclei of an organism's cells is species-specific. Human diploid cells (those that are not gametes) have 46 chromosomes. The number may be as low as 2, as in some ants and roundworms, or more than a thousand, as in the Indian fern Ophioglossum reticulatum, which has 1,260 chromosomes. So the number of chromosomes in a species does not correlate with the complexity of the organism.
2. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)

The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of flattened sacs and branching tubules that extends throughout the cytoplasm in plant and animal cells. These sacs and tubules are called cisternae (singular cisterna). All cisternae are interconnected, so the ER has only one large and highly convoluted lumen, the cisternal space, which takes up more than 10 percent of the total volume of a cell. The cisternae are also connected to the double-layered nuclear envelope, so the ER provides a pipeline between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. The ER manufactures, processes and transports a wide variety of biochemical compounds for use inside and outside the cell. There are two kinds: rough and smooth.

blocks.title: ER and nucleus share one compartment
blocks.text: Because of their physical membranous connection, the lumen of the ER and the space between the layers of the nuclear envelope form a single compartment. This close association lets the ER and the nucleus share information very efficiently.

blocks.alt: Part of a nucleus on the left. Four flattened rough ER cisternae studded with orange ribosomes stack next to it, the top one continuous with the nuclear envelope. To the right, smooth ER is a network of branching tubules without ribosomes. A small vesicle buds from the rough ER with an arrow towards the Golgi apparatus.
blocks.caption: Rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum joined to the nuclear envelope (original diagram after Figures 3.15 and 3.16).
blocks.long_description: Rough ER is a stack of flattened cisternae whose outer surface carries ribosomes; it makes and processes proteins and is continuous with the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope. Smooth ER is a network of tubules without ribosomes that makes lipids, stores calcium and detoxifies drugs. All cisternae share one lumen, the cisternal space. Transport vesicles bud from the ER and carry products to the Golgi apparatus.

blocks.text: The surface of the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) is covered with ribosomes, giving it a bumpy appearance under the microscope. It is involved mainly in the production and processing of proteins. During processing, the RER adds other chemicals (for example sugars) to the proteins, then transports the processed proteins to the areas of the cell where they are needed, or sends them to the Golgi apparatus for further processing and modification.

The surface of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) lacks ribosomes, so it appears more even under the microscope. In most cells it is much less extensive than the rough ER. The SER is chiefly involved in the production of lipids, building blocks for carbohydrate metabolism, and the detoxification of drugs and poisons. It also stores calcium and carries out calcium metabolism; in muscle cells the SER releases calcium to trigger muscle contraction.

blocks.title: Where smooth ER is abundant
blocks.text: Smooth ER is much more extensive in cells that do a lot of lipid and carbohydrate metabolism (brain and muscle) or detoxification (liver).
3. Ribosomes

All living cells contain ribosomes, tiny granular structures composed of approximately 60 percent ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and 40 percent protein. Ribosomes are not bound by a membrane and are much smaller than other organelles. In eukaryotic cells they are mainly found attached to the rough ER, with some scattered freely; in prokaryotic cells all ribosomes are freely scattered in the cytoplasm. Ribosomes are the protein production machinery of the cell and are most abundant in cells active in protein synthesis, such as pancreas and brain cells. A typical cell contains several thousand ribosomes, but some cell types have a few million.

Eukaryotic ribosomes are produced and assembled in the nucleolus. Ribosomal proteins enter the nucleolus and combine with rRNA strands to create the two ribosomal subunits, one small and one large. The subunits leave the nucleus through the nuclear pores, and in the cytoplasm the two combine for protein synthesis. When protein synthesis is not being done, the two subunits separate.

Protein synthesis requires the assistance of two other kinds of RNA molecule besides rRNA. Messenger RNA (mRNA) provides the instructions, which it has taken from the DNA. Transfer RNA (tRNA) brings amino acids to the ribosome. Once the chain of amino acids has been synthesised, the ribosome releases it.

blocks.title: Svedberg values
blocks.text: The subunits of a ribosome are described by their Svedberg (S) values, based on their rate of sedimentation in a centrifuge. The complete eukaryotic ribosome is 80S: a smaller 40S subunit and a larger 60S subunit. Prokaryotic cells have 70S ribosomes, each of a 30S and a 50S subunit. Svedberg values are not additive, because the rate of sedimentation depends on a molecule's size and shape rather than simply its molecular weight.

blocks.title: Free and bound ribosomes; ribosomes in organelles
blocks.text: Proteins synthesised by free ribosomes are for the cell's own internal use, while proteins made by ribosomes bound to the RER are transported out of the cell. Ribosomes are also found inside mitochondria and the chloroplasts of plants; these differ in size and make-up from cytoplasmic ribosomes and are more like those of prokaryotes.
4. Mitochondria

Mitochondria (singular mitochondrion) are rod-shaped organelles considered the power generators of the cell. A mitochondrion is bounded by two membranes with a narrow intermembrane space between them; beneath the inner membrane is the larger internal matrix. The outer membrane is smooth and acts like a sieve, filtering out molecules that are too big. The inner membrane is highly convoluted and forms many infoldings called cristae, which increase the surface area. The inner surface of the cristae has knob-like extensions into the matrix, the F1 particles; these are the enzyme ATP synthase. Other complexes in the inner membrane serve as electron carriers in the electron transport chain.

blocks.alt: A rod-shaped mitochondrion cut lengthwise: a smooth orange outer membrane, a pale intermembrane space, a dark inner membrane folded into several cristae that project into the cream-coloured matrix. Small green knobs (F1 particles) stud the cristae; a purple ring of circular DNA and three orange ribosomes lie in the matrix.
blocks.caption: Structure of a mitochondrion (original diagram after Figure 3.19).
blocks.long_description: The outer membrane is smooth and sieve-like. The inner membrane is folded into cristae that greatly increase its surface area and carry the F1 particles (ATP synthase) and the electron transport chain. The matrix inside holds the enzymes of the Krebs cycle, the mitochondrion's own circular DNA and its 70S ribosomes. The narrow intermembrane space lies between the two membranes.

blocks.text: Mitochondria differ from most other organelles: a mitochondrion has its own circular DNA (similar to the DNA of prokaryotes), all kinds of RNA and 70S ribosomes, and it can replicate independently of the cell. Mitochondria are the sites of cellular respiration. They generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) from oxygen and nutrients; ATP is the chemical energy "currency" that powers the cell's metabolic activities. Enzymes in the matrix catalyse some steps of cellular respiration, such as the Krebs cycle; the proteins of the electron transport chain are in the inner membrane.

blocks.title: How many, and where
blocks.text: The number of mitochondria in a cell depends on its metabolic requirements and ranges from one to thousands. Mitochondria are found in nearly all eukaryotes (plants, animals, fungi and protists) and are large enough to be seen with a light microscope. Scientists hypothesise that millions of years ago small free-living prokaryotes were engulfed, but not consumed, by larger prokaryotes; the two developed a symbiotic relationship, the larger providing nutrients and the smaller providing ATP.
5. Chloroplasts

One of the most important characteristics of plants is their ability to conduct photosynthesis, that is to make their own food by converting light energy into chemical energy. This occurs in almost all plant species and is carried out in specialised organelles, the chloroplasts. All the green structures in plants, including stems and unripened fruit, contain chloroplasts, but most photosynthetic activity in most plants occurs in the leaves. On average the chloroplast density on a leaf surface is about half a million per square millimetre. Chloroplasts contain the pigments chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b, which absorb the light energy needed for photosynthesis.

blocks.title: Recalling: plastids
blocks.text: Cells of plants and many protists have three types of plastid: chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts. The colourless leucoplasts are involved in storage; the yellow-to-red chromoplasts give colour to plant parts.

The ellipsoid chloroplast is enclosed by two membranes, with the intermembrane space between them. A semi-fluid called the stroma lies inside the inner membrane; it contains dissolved enzymes and makes up most of the chloroplast's volume. The outer membrane is much more permeable than the inner one. The inner membranes lie close together and fuse along their peripheries, so two adjacent membranes form a disc-shaped compartment called a thylakoid. Many thylakoids form stacks called grana (singular granum); the lamellae are the non-green compartments that connect two grana. Each granum may contain a few to several thylakoids, and a chloroplast may contain a hundred or more grana. Like the mitochondrion, the chloroplast has its own DNA and reproduces independently of the cell.

blocks.alt: An ellipsoid chloroplast cut lengthwise: a green outer membrane, a pale intermembrane space, an inner membrane and the pale green stroma. Inside are three stacks of flat discs (grana) joined by thin lamellae, a purple ring of circular DNA and a few orange ribosomes.
blocks.caption: Structure of a chloroplast (original diagram after Figure 3.20).
blocks.long_description: Two membranes enclose the chloroplast with an intermembrane space between them; the outer membrane is more permeable than the inner. The stroma is the enzyme-containing fluid inside, where carbon dioxide is turned into glucose. Thylakoids are disc-shaped compartments formed by fused inner membranes; stacks of thylakoids are grana, and lamellae connect one granum to the next. Chlorophyll a and b in the thylakoids absorb light. The chloroplast has its own circular DNA and ribosomes.

blocks.text: Light is absorbed by chlorophyll molecules embedded in the thylakoid discs. When these chlorophyll molecules absorb light they emit electrons, and thus ATP is formed. Using this ATP, in the stroma, low-energy carbon dioxide is transformed into a high-energy compound like glucose.

blocks.title: Mitochondria and chloroplasts compared
blocks.text: Both convert energy for the cell. Mitochondria perform aerobic respiration, generating ATP by metabolising sugars, fats and other fuels with the help of oxygen. Chloroplasts perform photosynthesis, converting energy from the sun into organic nutrients using carbon dioxide and water. Both contain their own DNA and grow and reproduce independently of the cell.
6. Golgi apparatus

The Golgi apparatus consists of five to eight cup-shaped, membrane-covered sacs called cisternae, stacked over each other. It is found in the cells of plants, animals and unicellular eukaryotes. In some unicellular flagellates the Golgi apparatus may consist of 60 cisternae, and the number of Golgi apparatuses in a cell varies with its function; animal cells generally contain between ten and twenty Golgi stacks. The complex is usually located close to the nucleus. Each Golgi stack has two distinct faces: the cis face is near the endoplasmic reticulum, and the trans face is positioned near the plasma membrane.

The Golgi apparatus is the distribution and shipping department for the cell's chemical products. It modifies the proteins and lipids built in the ER and prepares them for export outside the cell or for transport to other locations in the cell. Small vesicles containing proteins, carbohydrates, phospholipids and other molecules bud off from the ER and move through the cytoplasm until they reach the cis face of the Golgi apparatus, where they fuse and release their molecules into it. Here the compounds are further processed: enzymes in the Golgi lumen convert them into glycoproteins and glycolipids.

blocks.alt: Rough ER at the top sends two small vesicles down to the cis face of a stack of five curved cisternae. From the trans face at the bottom, secretory vesicles leave; one fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside, another becomes a lysosome.
blocks.caption: Structure of the Golgi apparatus and its functioning (original diagram after Figure 3.21).
blocks.long_description: Transport vesicles bud from the rough ER and fuse with the cis face of the Golgi stack. The contents pass through the five to eight cup-shaped cisternae, where enzymes modify them into glycoproteins and glycolipids. At the trans face, near the plasma membrane, products are packaged into vesicles: secretions leave the cell by exocytosis, other products return to the ER or mature into lysosomes.

blocks.text: The product is extruded from the trans face in a vesicle and directed to its final destination inside or outside the cell. The exported products are known as secretions. Other products are returned to the ER or may mature into lysosomes. In plant cells the Golgi apparatus also produces pectin and other polysaccharides needed for plant structure and metabolism.

blocks.title: Recalling: Camillo Golgi
blocks.text: Camillo Golgi, investigating the nervous system with a new staining technique (Golgi staining), observed a structure inside cells and named it the reticular apparatus. He announced his discovery in 1898 and the structure was named after him. Many scientists argued that it was a visual distortion caused by staining; the electron microscope in the twentieth century finally confirmed that the Golgi apparatus is a real organelle.
7. Lysosomes

Lysosomes are spherical organelles bounded by a single membrane. They serve as the digestive compartments of the cell and are found in most eukaryotic cells. In animals they are most numerous in disease-fighting cells such as white blood cells, which must digest bacteria, viruses and other foreign intruders. Lysosomes also break down cellular materials that have exceeded their lifetime or are no longer useful: this is autophagy. They break cellular waste products, fats, carbohydrates, proteins and other macromolecules into simple compounds, which are transferred back into the cytoplasm for making new materials.

Lysosomes have about 40 different hydrolytic enzymes, all manufactured in the ER and modified in the Golgi apparatus. The membrane covering of the lysosome protects the rest of the cell from these harsh digestive enzymes, which would otherwise cause significant damage.

blocks.title: Recalling: de Duve, and why the cell is safe
blocks.text: Lysosomes were discovered by the Belgian scientist Christian René de Duve. Investigating carbohydrate metabolism in liver cells, he observed that cells damaged in the centrifuge release acid phosphatase, and suggested that this digestive enzyme was encased in a membrane-bound organelle, which he named the lysosome. The lysosomal enzymes need an acidic environment (pH about 4.8). The lysosomal matrix is acidic but the cytosol is neutral, so even if a lysosome ruptures its enzymes become inactive and the cell remains uninjured.

blocks.title: Lysosomal storage diseases
blocks.text: In these diseases the patient lacks one of the hydrolytic enzymes of the lysosome, so the abnormal lysosome fills with indigestible substances that interfere with cellular functions. In Pompe's disease the lysosome lacks a glycogen-digesting enzyme, so harmful amounts of glycogen accumulate in liver cells. In Tay-Sachs disease an essential lipid-digesting enzyme is missing; lipids accumulate in the nerve cells of the brain, damage the nervous system, cause mental retardation and death in early childhood.

Lysosomes also function in the elimination of whole cells. Selective cell death is a mechanism multicellular organisms use in their development: when a tadpole develops into a frog, the cells of the tail are destroyed by lysosomal enzymes. Many cells in the brain die during development; this directed suicide is accomplished by the rupture of the lysosomes within the cells being eliminated.
8. Peroxisomes

Peroxisomes are single-membrane-bounded organelles in all eukaryotic cells, discovered by Christian de Duve, who also discovered lysosomes. Peroxisomes contain a variety of enzymes, many of them oxidative, carrying out oxidation (the removal of electrons and hydrogens). These enzymes primarily rid the cell of toxic substances; peroxisomes in liver cells, for example, detoxify alcohol and other harmful compounds by oxidising them. Some peroxisomes contain catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide (a common by-product of cellular metabolism) into water and oxygen.

blocks.title: Zellweger syndrome
blocks.text: Defects in peroxisomes cause a number of metabolic disorders. The most serious is Zellweger syndrome, characterised by the absence or reduced number of peroxisomes in cells. It is congenital (present at birth), has no cure or effective treatment, and usually causes death within the first year of life.
9. Glyoxysomes

Glyoxysomes are similar to peroxisomes but are found only in plant cells. They contain enzymes that convert lipids into carbohydrates. They are most abundant in the cells of lipid-rich seeds, such as castor beans and soya beans; during germination they convert stored lipids into carbohydrates that provide energy for seed germination.
10. Vacuoles

Vacuoles are membrane-bounded sacs that function in several ways. In mature plant cells a single large vacuole provides structural support and serves in storage, waste disposal, protection and growth. Vacuoles in animal cells are much smaller and are more commonly used to store materials temporarily or to transport substances. Many plant cells have a large, single central vacuole, which develops slowly by the fusion of smaller vacuoles and takes up most of the space in the cell (80 percent or more). It is enclosed by a membrane called the tonoplast, and the material inside is the cell sap, which differs markedly from the surrounding cytoplasm.

The central vacuole plays an important structural role related to its ability to control turgor pressure, which makes the rigidity of the cell. Under optimum conditions a plant receives adequate water and the central vacuoles of its cells swell as liquid collects in them, creating a high turgor pressure that helps maintain the structural integrity of the plant along with the support of the cell wall. Vacuoles also often store the pigments that give certain flowers their colours, which attract bees and other pollinators, and they release molecules poisonous to various insects and animals, discouraging them from eating the plant.

blocks.title: Recalling: vacuoles
blocks.text: Vacuoles are fluid-filled, single-membrane-bounded organelles. Cells have many small vacuoles in their cytoplasm; when a plant cell matures its small vacuoles fuse to form a single large vacuole. Several materials stored in plant vacuoles are useful to humans, such as opium, rubber and garlic flavouring.
11. Centrioles

In the cells of animals and most protists, centrioles are organelles associated with the assembly and organisation of the fibres of the cytoskeleton, the microtubules (including spindle fibres). In eukaryotic cells centrioles occur in pairs, the two located at right angles to one another near the nuclear envelope. In ciliated or flagellated cells centrioles are involved in the formation of cilia and flagella: each cilium and flagellum is anchored by a centriole, known as a basal body. The cells of plants and fungi lack centrioles and basal bodies; their microtubules and spindle fibres are organised from structures of the cytoplasm.

blocks.title: Recalling: centriole structure
blocks.text: Centrioles are hollow, cylindrical organelles. A centriole is made of nine triplets of microtubules.
12. Cytoskeleton
The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibres in the cytoplasm. It includes three types of fibre.

items: Microfilaments: present in all eukaryotic cells. They are solid rods made of the globular protein actin. Microfilaments disassemble and reassemble, helping cells to change shape and move; they enable a dividing cell to pinch off into two cells, and in association with myosin they help in cellular contraction.

Microtubules: straight, hollow cylinders composed of subunits, each made of two different tubulin proteins, alpha-tubulin and beta-tubulin. Microtubules give structure and shape to a cell and serve as highways for the transport of organelles. They are the major components of cilia and flagella and take part in forming the spindle fibres during cell division.

Intermediate filaments: found only in some higher animal groups. They are made of different proteins, the most common subunit being vimentin; some cells have intermediate filaments of other proteins, for example skin cells contain keratin. Intermediate filaments maintain cell shape and rigidity and anchor several organelles, including the nucleus.

blocks.alt: Three fibres side by side. Left, a microfilament: a twisted chain of orange actin beads. Middle, a microtubule: a hollow cylinder built of alternating blue alpha-tubulin and purple beta-tubulin subunits. Right, an intermediate filament: a rope of three twisted green protein strands. The functions of each are listed beneath.
blocks.caption: The three fibres of the cytoskeleton (original diagram after Figure 3.27).
blocks.long_description: Microfilaments are solid rods of actin about 7 nm across; they change cell shape, move the cell, pinch a dividing cell in two and contract with myosin. Microtubules are hollow cylinders of alpha- and beta-tubulin about 25 nm across; they give shape, act as highways for organelles, build cilia and flagella and form the spindle. Intermediate filaments are ropes of fibrous proteins such as vimentin or keratin about 10 nm across; they keep shape and rigidity and anchor organelles including the nucleus, and occur only in some animal groups.

blocks.text: 13. Cilia and flagella

A cilium (plural cilia) and a flagellum (plural flagella) are locomotor appendages that protrude from certain cells: thin, tail-like projections extending from the cell body. Cilia are short and usually numerous; flagella are longer but fewer. Cilia are rare in plants. Many protozoans (ciliates) possess cilia, and larger eukaryotes such as mammals have cilia on the surfaces of some cells; in humans, cilia line the trachea, where they sweep mucus and dirt out of the breathing tubes.

The core of a eukaryotic cilium or flagellum is the axoneme. It contains two central microtubules surrounded by an outer ring of nine doublet microtubules. Dynein molecules around the circumference of the axoneme bridge the gaps between adjacent doublets. Biologists call this organisation a "9 + 2" structure. A plasma membrane surrounds the entire axoneme. At the base of the cilium is its organising centre, the basal body, which has the same basic structure as the outer ring of the axoneme except that each of the nine outer sets is a triplet of microtubules rather than a doublet. The basal body is actually a centriole. Prokaryotic flagella have a completely different structure, built from the protein flagellin.

blocks.alt: Left, the cross-section of a cilium inside its plasma membrane: nine pairs of microtubules (blue and purple) in a ring with orange dynein arms between them, and two single green microtubules in the centre. Right, the cross-section of a basal body: nine triplets of microtubules in a ring with no central pair.
blocks.caption: The 9 + 2 axoneme of a eukaryotic cilium or flagellum, and its basal body (original diagram after Figures 3.26 and 3.28).
blocks.long_description: The axoneme has nine outer doublet microtubules around two central single microtubules, with dynein arms bridging neighbouring doublets, all enclosed by the plasma membrane. The basal body at the base is a centriole: nine triplets of microtubules and no central pair, hollow and cylindrical; centrioles occur in pairs at right angles near the nucleus. A prokaryotic flagellum is different, a filament of flagellin without microtubules.

blocks.prompt: Sort these into single-membrane, double-membrane and no-membrane structures: ribosome, lysosome, mitochondrion, Golgi apparatus, chloroplast, centriole, peroxisome, nucleus, vacuole.
blocks.explanation: Single membrane: lysosome, Golgi apparatus, peroxisome, vacuole. Double membrane: mitochondrion, chloroplast, nucleus. No membrane: ribosome, centriole.

blocks.prompt: Trace the path of a secretory protein from its synthesis to its release from the cell, naming the structures in order.
blocks.explanation: Ribosomes on the rough ER make the protein, which enters the cisternal space and is processed there (sugars added). It travels in a transport vesicle to the cis face of the Golgi apparatus, is modified into a glycoprotein as it passes through the cisternae, is packaged into a secretory vesicle at the trans face, and the vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane to release the secretion by exocytosis.

blocks.text: Quick recap

items: Cell wall: middle lamella (pectates) laid first, primary wall (cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin), secondary wall (lignin) in some cells; plasmodesmata join neighbouring plant cells. Fungi use chitin, bacteria peptidoglycan, diatoms silica.

Plasma membrane (fluid mosaic model, Singer and Nicolson 1972): phospholipid bilayer with proteins floating in it, cholesterol for fluidity, glycoproteins and glycolipids (glycocalyx) as identification marks; a semi-porous barrier.

Nucleus: double envelope with pore complexes, nuclear lamina, nucleoplasm, chromatin (DNA on histones, nucleosomes) that condenses into chromosomes (chromatids and centromere), nucleolus making ribosomal subunits at NORs. Chromosome number is species-specific and unrelated to complexity.

ER: rough (ribosomes, proteins) and smooth (lipids, detoxification, calcium); one cisternal space continuous with the nuclear envelope. Ribosomes: rRNA and protein, 80S (40S + 60S) in eukaryotes, 70S (30S + 50S) in prokaryotes.
Mitochondria (cristae, F1 particles, matrix, own DNA, 70S ribosomes) make ATP by respiration; chloroplasts (thylakoids, grana, lamellae, stroma, own DNA) make glucose by photosynthesis.

Golgi apparatus modifies and ships products (cis to trans); lysosomes digest (about 40 enzymes, acidic); peroxisomes oxidise toxins (catalase); glyoxysomes convert lipids to carbohydrates in seeds; vacuoles store and give turgor.

Centrioles (nine triplets, pairs at right angles) organise microtubules and anchor cilia and flagella as basal bodies; the cytoskeleton has microfilaments (actin), microtubules (tubulin) and intermediate filaments (vimentin, keratin); cilia and flagella have a 9 + 2 axoneme.
